label: paragraph_title
text: LONDON DIVORCE.

label: text
text: WIFE'S LETTERS FROM HONGKONG.

label: text
text: HUSBAND'S CHARGES.

label: text
text: "Concerning a wife eloped to China with her lodger and subsequently wrote in a repentant vein to her husband, a curious story was told in the Divorce Court," says the "News of the World" dated July 10. "Petitioner was Mr. Percy Laight, painter and decorator, of Beaconsfield Road, Stoke, Coventry. He alleged that his wife, Mrs. Eva Mary Laight, has committed misconduct with Mr. C. A. Sutherton Russ, a solicitor."

label: text
text:
Mr. Cotes-Preedy, K.C., explained that the parties were married in 1904, and there were three children. When petitioner returned home from military service in 1920 he found that Mr. Sutherton Russ was a lodger in the house. He had then no suspicions that there was anything wrong between his wife and co-respondent.
“In August, 1921, however, Mr. Laight received a letter from a firm of Coventry solicitors, with whom Mr. Russ was then employed, and on going there was informed that his wife had accused him of cruelty, and that he must enter into a deed of separation. In the presence of his wife and Mr. Russ, Mr. Laight was persuaded to enter into a deed of separation.

label: text
text:
"Afterwards Mrs. Laight and co-respondent left the house, and then it was that the husband's suspicions were aroused." He heard nothing more of his wife until he received a letter from her from Hongkong, in which she expressed her sorrow for being so wicked and heartless and saying she guessed petitioner had heard with whom she was. Later, Mr. Laight learned that Mr. Russ had obtained the steamship berths for respondent and the youngest son, whom she had taken with her. Mrs. Laight further wrote that she was a very unhappy woman, constantly thinking about the two sons she had left behind, adding, 'I was not mistress of myself,' and asking her husband's forgiveness.
"In sumport of his contention"

label: text
text: “In support of his contention that Mrs. Laight's letters from Hongkong inferred that she and Mr. Russ were living together, Mr. Cotes-Preedy read a letter she had written to a friend, in which she stated:

label: text
text: “In two years’ time we shall be rich, as we have these shares which will finish in 1925. Then we shall get £10,000, and there is Mr. Russ’s business.”

label: text
text: “Counsel added, with regard to the deed of separation, that Mr. Laight entirely repudiated the allegation that he had ever been cruel to his wife.”

label: text
text: “When Mr. Laight was giving evidence as to the deed of separation, Mr. Justice Hill asked: 'Is your wife much bigger than you?'”

label: text
text:
"Petitioner: 'No, my lord."
"His Lordship: 'I was wondering why you did it."

label: text
text:
“The jury found that respondent and co-respondent had committed misconduct and fixed damages at an agreed sum of $400.
“His Lordship therefore granted a decree nisi to Mr. Laight, with the damages.”

label: text
text: SUCCESSFUL RAIDE IN KOWLOON

label: text
text: FIVE PERSONS ARRESTED.

label: text
text: Armed with a search warrant, a party of Police under Sub-Inspector F. Shaftain paid a visit yesterday to the second floor of 47, Yu Chau Street, Kowloon, which was suspected to be harbouring suspicious characters.

label: text
text: The raid proved successful as two revolvers, 69 rounds of ammunition, and a quantity of gold watches and other jewellery were found on the premises.

label: text
text: As a sequel to the discovery of the arms and jewellery, three men and two women were taken into custody on suspicion that they had participated in an armed robbery at Hunghom on July 30.

label: paragraph_title
text: RENT INCREASE.

label: paragraph_title
text: COURT KEPT BUSY WITH DISTRAINTS.

label: paragraph_title
text: HARDSHIP ALLEGED.

label: text
text: Without expressing an opinion one way or the other, writes a correspondent to the "China Mail," there is certainly some distress in the matter of payment of rent during the last few weeks—a matter to which attention has again been drawn by the report in yesterday's issue of the latest action of the Chinese Tenants Association.

label: text
text: Every day, the writer maintains, the outdoor staff of the Supreme Court is busy attending to applications for distraint for rent. Being engaged in legal work he says that he knows for a fact that in normal times these applications seldom number more than four or five a day, but the number has now risen to about twenty a day.

label: text
text: A shroff, who is connected with the correspondent's client, has been to Court every day this week taking out distraints for rent in different parts of Hengkong.

label: text
text: The correspondent attributes this abnormal state of affairs to the hardship entailed by the poorest classes of Chinese who are hard put to live when food is so high. The number of instances where principal and sub-tenants have absconded wholesale will be surprising. With conditions as they are it is only to be expected that landlords have to take steps to recover back rent. "If, then," continues the writer, "the poor cannot pay back rent, how cfin they pay the increase of 15 per cent."

label: text
text:
Yesterday the “China Mail” reported that the Chinese Tenants Association had decided to petition the Government with a view to deferring the enforcement of the new rents law whereby an increase of 15 per cent on the standard rent is permissible. The “Wah Kiu Yat Po” yesterday reported that a number of landlords had been stated as having waived the right to increase for the time being.
To-day it is mentioned that legal advice is being sought in drawing up the petition.

label: text
text:
On inquiry the "China Mail" learns that the number of warrants issued is higher than normal. Amounts vary from trivial to fairly large sums. Some warrants have been executed after a few days' overlap and others when two or three months rent is outstanding.
In town this week were notified a good many small-size business establishments where the nation has been right to enter the market.

label: paragraph_title
text: COOLIE'S JEERS.

label: text
text: RICSHA MAN'S "CHNEK."

label: text
text: That after refusing to take him as a fare, a Kowloon ricsha coolie hid behind a tree and jeered at him, was the allegation made by Mr. J. P. Robinson, the well-known resident and cricketer, before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Yaumati Police Court this morning when the coolie was fined $10 or 14 days.

label: text
text:
The charge was one of refusing to accept a fare. Mr. Robinson came out of the Palace. Hotel about 1.45 p.m. yesterday and hailed the coolie who, sitting in his ricsha, refused. On Mr. Robinson's going over towards him, the coolie backed away, shouting, and pointing to the Hotel, indicating that he was engaged by a patron who had gone inside and was still waiting. Mr. Robinson then went inside where there was only one visitor who said that he did not have a ricsha waiting in the road. Mr. Robinson then insisted that the coolie should also go into the Hotel when his statement could be disproved but he hid behind the tree and jeered. He was handed over to an Indian police officer.
His Worship found the charge proved and imposed sentence as stated.

label: text
text:
Bad Language Used.
Lieut. Col. E. D. Matthews, secretary of the Golf Club, successfully prosecuted in another case, the ricsha coolie being fined $5 or 7 days for using bad language.

label: text
text: Giving evidence, Colonel Matthews said that he engaged defendant's vehicle at the Kowloon "Star" Ferry wharf at 1 p.m. on August 4 to go to Humphrey's Building. In Mody Road defendant went very slowly and wandered from one side to the other of the road. Witness told him to "Faitee" (Hurry Up!) whereupon defendant turned round and used the words complained of.

label: text
text: Defendant denied the charge. His version was that when his fare told him to get a move on, he turned round and answered "Ho" (Good).

label: text
text:
His Worship (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) said that defendant was lying as there was all the difference between the monosyllabic "Ho" and the epithets which Colonel Matthews had heard.
His Worship also remarked that it was lucky for defendant that the/ Colonel had taken his number and applied for a summons otherwise he (defendant) might have been worse off.

label: paragraph_title
text: A "CRUEL MURDER."

label: text
text: After a retirement of half an hour's duration, the jury found guilty of murder a Chinese against whom it was alleged that in conjunction with another man he had caused the death of an Indian constable. According to the dying statement of the Indian constable, the prisoner and another man, with a view to obtaining possession of the revolver he carried, had stabbed him and then shot him with his own revolver.

label: text
text: sentence of death, said the evidence against prisoner was very clear and he was fully in accord with the verdict, which had been given. Prisoner had been found guilty of taking part in a very cruel murder. The unfortunate constable had done nothing to prisoner and simply because two men wanted possession of his revolver they murdered him in the way they did. He then passed sentence of death, prisoner showing no signs of emotion, walking quietly from the lock.

label: text

CHANG TSO-LIN SENDS
TROOPS.

label: text
text: FALSE REPORTS CIRCULATED.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The Yuta mill, which was wrecked, is owned by Japanese. The Paocheng mill, where the strike started, is partly wrecked and is Chinese owned and American managed. No further disturbances have taken place today. A number of workmen presented themselves at the mills, but it will probably be months before the Yuta mill is working.

label: text
text:
A detachment of special gender-darmerie, sent from Mukden by Chang Tso-lin, has arrived.
It is stated that a number of students and strike leaders have found refuge in the Foreign Concessions.

label: text
text: Twenty rioters and nine police who were wounded, have been admitted to hospital in the native city. Five of the former are reported to have very little chance of recovery, whilst some of the police are not expected to live. It appears that many of the wounded were carried to the country, fearing arrest.

label: text
text: Many false reports have been circulated among Chinese, in which foreigners are blamed for the trouble.

label: paragraph_title
text: SOLD FOR $650

label: text
text: FATE OF MR. ABBOT'S MANILA PURCHASE.

label: paragraph_title
text: TO MEET STORAGE CHARGES.

label: text
text: The Curtis biplane, which Mr. H. W. Abbott brought from Manila in March of this year and has since been lying partially submerged off the Empress wharf at the Kowloon Godowns, was sold by auction this morning on the instructions of the Pacific Main Steamship Company, which is winding up its affairs here. Instructions for sale were given in order to defray cost of storage.

label: text
text: The biplane was the one which broke from its moorings at Manila and was recovered slightly damaged after many hours drifting out to sea. Mr. Abbott, who was in Manila at the time, bought it with the intention of demonstrating the practicability of instituting a passenger and mail service between Hongkong and Shanghai, but since its arrival it has received no attention; and, although the fabric showed little signs of deterioration at the sale this morning, the hull and other parts were not in the best condition. Since one of the recent "blows" the machine has remained partially capsized.

label: text
text: The chief value lay in twin 12 cylinder engines, Liberty motors, which are tremendously powerful, for the 'plane was designed to carry sixteen or eighteen. These motors will naturally be very expensive to run.

label: text
text: The sale of the plane this morning was conducted by Mr. L. E. Lammert, of Lammert Bros. Mr. Rowe and Mr. A. Wing, the latter of whom salvaged the Heung Shan, were the only bidders, and the price advanced from $550 to $650, at which figure the plane was bought by Mr. Rowe. The sale was subject to the restrictions on removal from the Colony in connection with which permission will have to be obtained from the Superintendent of Imports and Exports.

label: text
text: WIL KELLEY MOTHER'S FEARS

label: paragraph_title
text: TRAIN DISASTER.

label: text
text:
HEAVY CASUALTY LIST.
WORST FOR LONG TIME.
(Reuter's Service.)

label: paragraph_title
text: Paris, August 13.

label: text
text: The Boulogne express-traveling at full speed was derailed near Amiens.

label: text
text: Nine people were killed and 50 injured.

label: text
text: FURTHER DETAILS.

label: text
text: It is known that 12 were killed and 80 injured.

label: text
text: The engine driver has been arrested.

label: text
text: The train was unusually full of holiday-makers, mostly third class, going to the seaside.

label: text
text: The train was due to stop at Amiens, but entered the station at full speed.

label: text
text:
The engine jumped the points and dragged off the luggage van and seven third class coaches, which telescoped and splintered.
M. Briand, returning from London, was held up as a consequence of the accident, causing rumours in Paris that it was his train that has been derailed. Actually M. Briand's train arrived a few minutes after the disaster and was delayed outside Amiens while casualties were removed from the wreckage, which was subsequently hauled slowly to another track at Amiens station, showing horrified passengers; the results of one of the worst accidents in France for a long time.

label: paragraph_title
text: Total Casualties:

label: text
text: Latest details of the rail smash show nine killed and 160 injured, of which 71 are serious, three not expected to survive.

label: paragraph_title
text: Excessive Speed

label: text
text:
It appears that the driver of the wrecked train entered the station at 56 miles an hour instead of the usual 26 after which he applied the brake too suddenly.
Heartrending cries emerged from the smashed timber and tangled ironwork, from which mangled corpses were extricated. The horror of the scene was increased by three coaches catching fire, which was extinguished, thanks to the splendid work of the Fire Brigade.

label: text

LIGHT IN WIGHT
REALLY WATERROOF

label: text
text: An official statement says that the President having decided to separate from his wife, issued a decree of divorce as from August 5. Reasons are not given, but rumour has been busy for some time. The step is attributed in some quarters to a tendency of masterfulness and a desire to participate in matters outside her sphere on the part of a young wife who has been educated in England and France, and was leader of the Turkish Women's Emancipation prior to the marriage.

label: text
text: A serious split was evident a fortnight ago when the wife hurriedly left Angora to rejoin her parents. All the Commissioners then saw her off, the President being the only absentee.

label: text
text:
Mustapha Kemal, President of the Turkish Republic, has informed the Government that he has divoced his wife, Latife Hanoum.
